pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is a method in Go, and how does it differ from a plain function? Where does the receiver go in the declaration?
expected_points: a method is a function with a receiver parameter written between func and the name
called with the dot syntax on a value of the receiver type
otherwise an ordinary function — no hidden behavior; it groups behavior with the type and namespaces the name per type

questions.prompt: You are adding a method to a type. How do you decide between `func (t T)` and `func (t *T)`? Give your rules.
expected_points: mutation of the receiver requires a pointer receiver
large structs called often favor a pointer to avoid copying every field
otherwise prefer a value receiver — it promises the call cannot change the caller's data
consistency convention: if any method needs a pointer receiver, give the type pointer receivers throughout

questions.prompt: A teammate writes `func (a Account) Deposit(amount int) { a.Balance += amount }` and the balance never changes. Explain to them exactly why.
expected_points: the receiver is passed by value like every argument, so a is a field-by-field copy
the method mutates the copy, which is discarded when it returns
a pointer receiver makes the receiver refer to the caller's Account, so the write lands in the shared value

questions.prompt: What is in the method set of `T`, what is in the method set of `*T`, and why does `*T` get more?
expected_points: method set of T: the value-receiver methods
method set of *T: value-receiver and pointer-receiver methods — everything
a pointer can always reach its value by dereferencing, but a value does not always have an address to offer a pointer method

questions.prompt: `acc` is a variable of type `Account` and `Withdraw` has receiver `*Account`. Why does `acc.Withdraw(10)` compile, and when would that same call shape fail?
expected_points: the compiler rewrites it to (&acc).Withdraw(10) because acc is addressable
it fails on non-addressable values, e.g. Account{...}.Withdraw(10) on a literal or m[key].Withdraw(10) on a map element

questions.prompt: Why did the exercise define `type Cents int` instead of hanging `Dollars` directly on `int`?
expected_points: methods can only be declared on named types defined in the same package
you cannot add methods to built-ins or to types another package owns
the named type also documents meaning and requires explicit conversion like Cents(1234)
